title: Common Flowchart Mistakes
objectives: Recognize common flowchart mistakes (open branches, a process with two exits)
Judge whether a flowchart is valid

hook.text: A flowchart that merely "looks nice" is not enough. If it breaks the rules, it represents an algorithm that does not work at all.

concept.heading: Open branches
concept.body: BOTH exits of a decision (IF) symbol (Yes/No) must lead somewhere. If a branch is left "hanging in the air" with no connection, what happens in that case stays unclear, and the flowchart is invalid.

concept.heading: A process with two exits
concept.body: A process (rectangle) symbol must have ONLY ONE exit. If two arrows leave a process, that is a design mistake: the only symbol that allows more than one exit is the decision (diamond).

exercises.question: What happens if the "No" exit of an IF symbol is not connected to anything?
options: Nothing, the output is empty automatically
The flowchart is invalid because what happens in that case stays unclear
The program runs twice as fast
The "No" case never happens

feedback.correct: Correct. Every decision branch must lead somewhere, otherwise the flow is unclear.
feedback.incorrect: An unconnected branch leaves it unclear what happens when that case is reached, so the flowchart is invalid.

exercises.question: What does it mean when two different arrows leave a process (rectangle) symbol?
options: It is normal
The process symbol should really have been a decision symbol: a design mistake
Two operations are being done at the same time
The flowchart runs faster

feedback.correct: Correct. Only the decision (diamond) symbol allows more than one exit.
feedback.incorrect: A process symbol must have a single exit. If more than one exit is needed, there should be a decision symbol there.

exercises.question: What happens if a flowchart has no "End" terminal at all?
options: The flowchart is valid, no problem
It is unclear when the algorithm ends, so the finiteness property is violated
The flowchart is completed automatically
It is only a visual omission, there is no logical problem

feedback.correct: Correct. Without an "End", there is no guarantee that the algorithm finishes.
feedback.incorrect: Without an "End" terminal, the algorithm's finiteness property (that it ends at some point) cannot be met.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.template: Both branches (Yes and No) of a decision symbol must be ___ to something.
options: connected
empty
colored
broken

exercises.question: Two decision symbols are connected one after the other. Which statement is true?
options: This is valid, nested decisions are normal
Decisions in a row are always forbidden
Only terminal symbols can come one after another
Process symbols can never come after a decision

feedback.correct: Correct. Nested (consecutive) decisions are completely valid. You will see this in detail in 3.3.
feedback.incorrect: Consecutive or nested decisions are valid; the flowchart rules do not forbid them.

exercises.question: Is it a mistake when more than one arrow ENTERS the same symbol in a flowchart (for example, the start of a loop)?
options: Yes, it is always a mistake
No, this is normal in loops and where branches merge
It is a mistake only for terminal symbols
It is a mistake only for decision symbols

feedback.correct: Correct. More than one arrow entering a symbol (e.g. the start of a loop) is completely normal.
feedback.incorrect: More than one arrow can enter a symbol. This is normal in loops and where branches merge. The mistakes are in the EXIT arrows breaking the rule.

summary: Every decision branch (Yes/No) must lead somewhere.
A process symbol can have only one exit. If more than one exit is needed, there must be a decision there.
Every flowchart must have exactly one Start and at least one End.
